title: Should you put your iPhone in rice?
caption:
Don't put your iPhone in rice. Apple's own support page says so.
Tiny rice bits could damage it. Here's what Apple says to do instead.
Ever put a phone in rice? Yes or no?

pinned_comment: Short version: Apple's own support page says "Don't put your iPhone in a bag of rice. Doing so could allow small particles of rice to damage your iPhone." Instead: tap it gently against your hand with the connector facing down, leave it in a dry area with some airflow, and don't charge it while it's wet. Ever put a phone in rice? Yes or no?

pinned_backups.reply: Apple's page doesn't say whether rice dries a phone. It says don't use it, and why: "Doing so could allow small particles of rice to damage your iPhone." It's on the same list as heat, compressed air and cotton swabs.

pinned_backups.if: How long should I wait before charging?
pinned_backups.reply: Apple's two pages put it differently. The liquid-alert page (102643): "After at least 30 minutes, try charging" and "It might take up to 24 hours to fully dry." The water-resistance page (108039): "Allow at least 5 hours before charging with a Lightning or USB-C cable or connecting an accessory." If the alert comes back, it's still wet.

pinned_backups.if: What if I need to charge it right now?
pinned_backups.reply: Apple's page: "you have the option in an emergency to override the liquid detection and charge your iPhone." It also says "If you have a wireless charger, you can still use that to charge your iPhone", once the back is dry. The risk of charging a wet port: "the pins on the connector or cable can corrode".

pinned_backups.if: Can I use a hair dryer?
pinned_backups.reply: Apple: "Don't dry your iPhone using an external heat source or compressed air." What its water-resistance page does suggest: "Placing your iPhone in front of a fan blowing cool air directly into the Lightning or USB-C connector might help the drying process."

pinned_backups.if: My iPhone says Liquid Detected but it's dry.
pinned_backups.reply: Apple's page: "If you see this alert every time you connect a certain cable or accessory, that cable or accessory might be damaged. Contact the manufacturer." If it happens with every Apple cable or accessory, "you might need service."
We only read Apple's iPhone pages, so the video makes no claim about other phones. Check your phone maker's own support page.

youtube_description:
Don't put your iPhone in rice. That's Apple's own advice: "Don't put your iPhone in a bag of rice. Doing so could allow small particles of rice to damage your iPhone."
So what should you do with a wet iPhone? Tap it gently against your hand with the connector facing down, leave it in a dry area with some airflow, and don't charge it while it's wet. Apple's liquid-alert page says it might take up to 24 hours to fully dry.

Apple's list of things not to do, from "If you see a liquid-detection alert on your iPhone": "Don't dry your iPhone using an external heat source or compressed air. Don't insert a foreign object, such as a cotton swab or a paper towel, into the connector. Don't put your iPhone in a bag of rice. Doing so could allow small particles of rice to damage your iPhone." Apple says rice "could" damage it; the page doesn't say whether rice dries a phone.

Why not charge it wet: "If you charge your iPhone while the Lightning or USB-C connector is wet, the pins on the connector or cable can corrode and cause permanent damage or stop functioning". In an emergency, Apple says "you have the option in an emergency to override the liquid detection and charge your iPhone."

How to dry it (same page): "Tap your iPhone gently against your hand with the connector facing down to remove excess liquid. Leave your iPhone in a dry area with some airflow." Apple's water-resistance page adds: "Placing your iPhone in front of a fan blowing cool air directly into the Lightning or USB-C connector might help the drying process."

How long to wait? Apple's two pages put it differently. The liquid-alert page (102643): "After at least 30 minutes, try charging with a Lightning or USB-C cable or connecting an accessory." and "It might take up to 24 hours to fully dry." The water-resistance page (108039): "Allow at least 5 hours before charging with a Lightning or USB-C cable or connecting an accessory."

Check yours: try charging later. Apple: "If you see the alert again, there is still liquid in the connector or under the pins of your cable." The alert works on "iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, or later".

Fine print: This video is about iPhone only and makes no claim about other phones. The search bar, the Apple support page card, the page clippings and the Liquid Detected alert are re-created by hand from Apple's wording; the rice-on-pins drawing is our illustration, and the phone is generic. Not affiliated with Apple.
